deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is the opening of Pars secunda of Riemann's 1861 Paris prize essay on heat conduction (the 'Commentatio mathematica'). The physical problem: for a homogeneous body the conductivities are constant. Riemann therefore asks when the quadratic form Σ b_{ιι'}(s) ds_ι ds_{ι'} can be turned into a form Σ a_{ιι'} dx_ι dx_{ι'} with constant coefficients by substituting s = s(x).

Step 0 (reduction). A positive definite form with constant coefficients can be reduced by a linear change of variables to Σ dx_ι². So the question becomes: when is Σ b_{ιι'} ds_ι ds_{ι'} = Σ dx_ν², i.e. when is the metric b flat?

Step 1 (notation). B = det(b), and β_{ιι'} are the cofactors. Then Σ_ι β_{ιι'} b_{ιι''} = B·δ_{ι'ι''}, so b^{-1} = β/B. The sign ≷ on the page means 'unequal'.

Step 2 (polarisation). Put J_{νι} = ∂x_ν/∂s_ι and K = ∂s/∂x = J^{-1}. The identity Σ b ds ds = Σ dx² holds for all dx. Replacing d by d+δ and comparing the cross terms gives the bilinear identity Σ b_{ιι'} ds_ι δs_{ι'} = Σ_ν dx_ν δx_ν, i.e. b = J^T J.

Step 3, equation (1): ∂x_{ν'}/∂s_ν = Σ_ι b_{νι} ∂s_ι/∂x_{ν'}. This is J^T = bK.

Step 4, equation (2): inverting with cofactors gives ∂s_ι/∂x_{ν'} = Σ_ν (β_{νι}/B) ∂x_{ν'}/∂s_ν. This is K = b^{-1}J^T.

Step 5. Using KJ = I (Σ_ν ∂s_ι/∂x_ν · ∂x_ν/∂s_{ι'} = δ_{ιι'}) one obtains:
- (3) Σ_ν ∂x_ν/∂s_ι · ∂x_ν/∂s_{ι'} = b_{ιι'}, i.e. b = J^T J;
- (4) Σ_ν ∂s_ι/∂x_ν · ∂s_{ι'}/∂x_ν = β_{ιι'}/B, i.e. KK^T = b^{-1}.

Step 6. Differentiate (3) with respect to s_{ι''}:
Σ_ν x_{ν,ιι''} x_{ν,ι'} + Σ_ν x_{ν,ι'ι''} x_{ν,ι} = ∂b_{ιι'}/∂s_{ι''}.

Step 7. Write the same identity for the three cyclic arrangements and add the first two minus the third (my explicit bookkeeping). With A(a;b,c) = Σ_ν x_{ν,bc} x_{ν,a}, the terms that are symmetric in the last two indices cancel. This gives equation (5):
2 Σ_ν x_{ν,ι'ι''} x_{ν,ι} = ∂_{ι''} b_{ιι'} + ∂_{ι'} b_{ιι''} − ∂_ι b_{ι'ι''} =: p_{ι,ι',ι''}.
This is twice the Christoffel symbol of the first kind [ι'ι'',ι].

Outlook (next page). Combining with (4) gives (6): 2 x_{ν,ι'ι''} = Σ_ι (∂s_ι/∂x_ν) p_{ιι'ι''}. A further differentiation and antisymmetrisation then yields the vanishing of the Riemann curvature tensor (ιι',ι''ι''') as the necessary condition for flatness.
errors: Riemann writes 'differentiando formulam posteriorem', but the formula actually differentiated is (3), the earlier ('prior') one. A later hand in the margin queries this with '(priorem?)'. It is a verbal slip; the mathematics is right.
In the differentiated formula and in (5), the index ν on x and the summation over ν are suppressed. This is notational shorthand, not an error.
All displayed steps (1)–(5) check out. (2) uses the symmetry of the cofactor matrix, which holds because b is symmetric.

results.what: Reduction of the homogeneous-conductor problem to the question of whether a metric Σ b ds ds is transformable into Σ dx², i.e. is flat
results.modern_name: Local flatness (equivalence) problem for Riemannian metrics
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (1854 Habilitation lecture, 1861 Paris essay); Christoffel and Lipschitz (1869–70) for the general equivalence problem

results.what: Formulas (1)–(4): b = J^T J and b^{-1} = (∂s/∂x)(∂s/∂x)^T via cofactors
results.modern_name: Metric pulled back by the Jacobian; inverse metric g^{ij}
Christoffel symbols of the first kind (Gauss formula for an embedded/flat-coordinate map)
results.usually_credited_to: Christoffel 1869 (with antecedents in Gauss, Lamé, Riemann)

deep.surprise_reason: This is the draft of Riemann's 1861 Paris prize essay. It was published in his Gesammelte Werke (1876), and historians routinely cite it as the first explicit computation of the curvature tensor and of the flatness criterion. The page itself contains only the standard preliminary identities leading to the Christoffel symbols. They are correct and well known to be in Riemann's essay.

transcription_corrections: 'si ι' ≷ ι''' and 'si ι ≶ ι'' both mean 'if the indices are unequal' (≠); the transcription is faithful.
In the title the coefficient b_{ι,ι'} carries an extra illegible superscript mark in the image; it should read simply b_{ι,ι'}.
The pencilled '(priorem?)' is a later marginal annotation beside 'differentiando formulam posteriorem', not part of Riemann's text.
The '42' in the right margin is the archival folio number; the page number written by Riemann is '12.'.
In the differentiated formula and in (5) the image shows x without index and Σ without a summation index. The implied sum is over ν (x_ν), which should be noted rather than silently restored.
